question: When's the last time you picked up something that was languishing; that wouldn't have happened without you?

raiseTranscript.text: When's the last time you picked up something that was languishing; that wouldn't have happened without you?

A ticket for updating our internal API docs had sat for four months. I noticed it while onboarding a new teammate who kept asking the same questions. I claimed it, rewrote the sections on auth flows, added examples, and got it reviewed.
What made you decide to take it instead of just answering the questions yourself?
The questions kept coming up in Slack. Fixing it once meant the next three people wouldn't need to ask. I also asked my manager if the time was okay since it wasn't on my sprint board.
How did you know it was actually used after?
The new hires stopped asking those questions and one of them left a comment on the doc saying it saved them a day.

raiseNotes: Q: When's the last time you picked up something that was languishing; that wouldn't have happened without you?
Junior dev noticed stale API docs ticket open 4 months
Claimed it during onboarding friction, added auth examples
Asked manager before pulling time from sprint
Outcome: new hires stopped repeating questions; doc comment cited time saved
Follow-up: Why take ownership vs just answering? - Said it scaled for future people
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate identified an unowned doc gap that directly slowed onboarding, claimed the ticket without being asked, and verified downstream impact through reduced questions. Quote: 'Fixing it once meant the next three people wouldn't need to ask.' This shows clear individual ownership and learning from repeated friction rather than treating it as someone else's problem. Biggest strength is proactive follow-through on a low-visibility item without manager prompting.

Our shared retry library had been flagged as risky for two quarters. No team owned the migration. I pulled the usage data, wrote a migration plan, convinced three service owners to adopt the new version in their next sprint, and drove the cutover.
What resistance did you hit?
One team said they had higher priorities. I showed them their p99 latency numbers tied to the old library and offered to pair on the change.
What was the measurable result?
Error rates from that path dropped 40% across the three services; we retired the old library entirely.

Drove cross-team migration with data and pairing offer
Pushed back on priority objections with latency evidence
Outcome: 40% error drop, old library retired
Follow-up: What resistance? - Offered to pair and showed numbers
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate surfaced an unowned cross-service risk, created a migration plan, influenced three teams without authority, and delivered a 40% error reduction. Quote: 'I showed them their p99 latency numbers tied to the old library.' This demonstrates ownership that spans teams plus concrete metrics. Biggest strength is turning a stalled item into measurable platform improvement through influence.

Our on-call rotation had high burnout and no clear escalation path. I created a new tiered model, got buy-in from the other managers, trained two new leads, and handed it off after the first quarter.
How did you handle the managers who pushed back?
Two thought it added overhead. I ran a 30-day pilot on one team showing reduced escalations to seniors and then shared the data.
What happened to the original problem?
Burnout survey scores improved 25 points and senior engineers reported fewer 2am pages.

We had no formal incident review process after major outages. I sponsored a blameless post-mortem program, funded tooling, and required it for any Sev-1. After six months it became the default across the org.
What trade-offs did you make?
I delayed two product launches by a sprint to free up the initial engineering time and accepted short-term velocity impact for long-term learning.
How do you know it stuck?
We now run 18 post-mortems per quarter with action items tracked in our planning system; repeat incidents in the same area dropped 60%.

raiseNotes: Q: When's the last time you picked up something that was languishing; that wouldn't have happened without you?

Funded tooling and mandated for Sev-1s
Accepted sprint delay trade-off for product launches
Outcome: 18 post-mortems/quarter, 60% drop in repeat incidents
Follow-up: What trade-offs? - Delayed launches for initial capacity
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate recognized the absence of a critical org process, invested resources despite product trade-offs, and embedded it into operating rhythm with measurable reduction in repeat incidents. Quote: 'I delayed two product launches by a sprint to free up the initial engineering time.' This demonstrates strategic ownership at scale with clear long-term judgment. Biggest strength is converting an unowned risk into durable cultural change.
